text: Sosoliso Airlines Flight 1145 (SO1145/OSL1145) was a scheduled domestic passenger flight from Abuja (ABV) to Port Harcourt (PHC), carrying 103 passengers and 7 crew members. The aircraft, a McDonnell Douglas DC-9-32 with serial number 47562/685, manufactured in 1972 and equipped with two Pratt & Whitney JT8D-9A engines, departed Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport at 12:25 p.m. on 10 December 2005. The flight was uneventful until its final approach, when, at approximately 14:08 local time (13:08 UTC), it crash-landed at Port Harcourt International Airport after descending below the minimum decision altitude of 307 feet (94 m) without visual contact with the runway. The crew had been cleared to descend to 4,900 metres (16,000 ft) and later requested weather information, receiving a report of scattered cumulonimbus clouds and no precipitation, though the controller failed to relay wind speed or the possibility of thunderstorms or wind shear. At 11 kilometres from the airport, the aircraft was on the glide-slope and requested landing clearance on Runway 21, with a warning about a potentially wet runway. As rain intensified and visibility deteriorated, Captain Benjamin Adebayo (48, with 10,050 total flight hours and 1,900 on the DC-9) called for a go-around at about 200 feet (61 m), approximately 100 feet below the decision altitude, but the aircraft was already too low to recover. The "TOO LOW-GEAR" warning sounded as the crew attempted to add thrust and reconfigure the aircraft, but the flaps and landing gear were not properly retracted. The DC-9 slammed onto a grass strip between the runway and taxiway, struck a concrete drainage culvert located about 70 meters to the left of Runway 21, and disintegrated, with fuel spilling and the aircraft bursting into flames. The fuselage and cockpit slid for hundreds of meters before coming to rest on the taxiway. Of the 110 people on board, only two survived: Kechi Okwuchi, a student from Loyola Jesuit College, who was treated in Johannesburg and Galveston, and Bunmi Amusan, who survived with 40% burns. All seven crew members and 59 of the 60 Loyola Jesuit College students died. The Nigerian Accident Investigation Bureau (AIB) attributed the crash to the crew's decision to continue descending past the decision altitude without visual contact, with contributing factors including adverse weather caused by microburst-induced wind shear and thunderstorms, the absence of runway lighting, improper execution of the go-around, and the lack of wind shear recognition in simulator training. The flight data recorder showed the aircraft leveled off at 204 feet (62 m), below the decision altitude, and continued descending, with a go-around attempt initiated but too late. The cockpit voice recorder confirmed the go-around call was made about 16 seconds before impact. The AIB concluded the probable cause was the crew's decision to continue the approach beyond the decision altitude without visual contact, with adverse weather as a contributing factor. The final report was published on 26 July 2006. The AIB recommended that wind shear recognition and recovery be made compulsory in pilot simulator training, a recommendation not implemented in time, leading to another crash a year later in Abuja. The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) mandates a compensation of 3 million naira (US$18,157) per family, and in January 2009, the Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) confirmed Sosoliso had paid $2.3 million into an escrow account. Pope Benedict XVI sent condolences to the families and offered prayers for relief workers. Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo cut short his visit to Portugal and pledged to overhaul the aviation sector, suspending several senior officials. The parents of victims Chuka, Nkem, and Busonma Ilabor founded the Ilabor Angels foundation to assist orphans and AIDS victims. Loyola Jesuit College established a Memorial Hall for the deceased students, created a Concerned Students Club, and founded Jesuit Memorial College in 2013 and Loyola Academy in 2014 to serve lower-income families. The runway lighting was only available under specific conditions due to unstable power supply and lack of funding. The flight recorders were damaged by impact and fire and were later analyzed in the UK. The crash was the second in Nigeria in under three months, following Bellview Airlines Flight 210 on 22 October 2005, which killed all 117 on board and was Sosoliso's first and only fatal accident.
